name: WR 124
description: WR 124 is the Wolf-Rayet star inside the nebula M1-67, about 6,400 parsecs away.

radius.source: Hamann et al. (2019), A&A 625, A57, Table 1, WR 124: R* = 11.93 solar radii, the radius where the continuum's Rosseland optical depth is 20 (Sect. 2), under the wind

temperature.source: Hamann et al. (2019), A&A 625, A57, Table 1, WR 124: T* = 44.7 kK, the temperature at that radius; spectral subtype WN8h

distance.source: Zavala et al. (2022), MNRAS 513, 3317, Sect. 1: an estimated distance of 6.4 (+2.5, −0.8) kpc, from Jiménez-Hernández et al. (2020), the distance its nebula's page stands at

limb.none: no limb-darkening grid describes a Wolf-Rayet star, whose light leaves an expanding wind, not a still atmosphere

color.reason: The star's measured light is reddened by dust between it and the Sun, a color excess E(b−v) of 1.08 mag (Hamann et al. 2019, Table 1): Gaia's spectrum shows that dust, not the star

text.card: WR 124 is the Wolf-Rayet star inside the nebula M1-67, about 6,400 parsecs away.
text.introduction: A star of 44,700 K with about 560,000 times the Sun's light, losing its mass in a wind of 710 km/s. The sphere drawn is the star under that wind.
text.locator: Table 1: WR 124, WN8h, T* = 44.7 kK, terminal wind velocity 710 km/s, R* = 11.93 Rsun, log(L/Lsun) = 5.75

notes: What is drawn is the star under its wind: the radius where the continuum's optical depth is 20 (Hamann et al. (2019), A&A 625, A57, Sect. 2, https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.04687). The wind above it is still opaque, and the paper prints no radius for where it turns clear.

The star's mass is not measured. Table 1 of the same paper gives 22 solar masses from a mass-luminosity relation for helium-burning stars and 20 from one built on evolutionary tracks (https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.04687).
Its wind: 710 km/s, carrying off 10^-4.3 solar masses a year (Table 1, https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.04687). The wind is not drawn.

The radius and luminosity are for the paper's own distance, a modulus of 14.0 (+0.5, −0.4) from Gaia DR2, 6.3 kpc (Table 1, https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.04687); the star stands here at its nebula's 6.4 kpc.

A compact companion hidden deep in the wind has been proposed; the paper keeps the star as single (Hamann et al. (2019), A&A 625, A57, comments on WR 124, https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.04687). It is drawn as one star.
Its light reaches us reddened by dust: a color excess E(b−v) of 1.08 mag (Table 1, https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.04687).

radialVelocity.source: SIMBAD's radial velocity for Gaia DR3 4513494205567536512 (quality D), from 2007AN....328..889K; Gaia DR3 measures none
